    !identical(utils::packageDescription("metatools")$RemoteSha, metatools_sha)) {
  pak::pak(paste0("ejlundgren/metatools@", metatools_sha))
}
library("metatools")

library("ggplot2")
library("data.table")
library("ggpattern")
library("patchwork")
library("metafor")
library("dplyr")
library("broom")
library("broom.mixed")

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false

# Arctic willow warming example from the 2.1 page (biomass in grams, n = 20 per group)
ctrl_m <- 10; ctrl_sd <- 2; n_w <- 20
warm_m <- 12; warm_sd <- 3

# Uncorrected definition formulas, so that lnCVR = lnVR - lnRoM holds exactly
lnRoM_w  <- as.numeric(escalc("ROM", m1i = warm_m, m2i = ctrl_m,
                              sd1i = warm_sd, sd2i = ctrl_sd,
                              n1i = n_w, n2i = n_w, correct = FALSE)$yi)
lnVR_w   <- as.numeric(escalc("VR", sd1i = warm_sd, n1i = n_w,
                              sd2i = ctrl_sd, n2i = n_w, correct = FALSE)$yi)
lnCVR_w  <- as.numeric(escalc("CVR", m1i = warm_m, m2i = ctrl_m,
                              sd1i = warm_sd, sd2i = ctrl_sd,
                              n1i = n_w, n2i = n_w, correct = FALSE)$yi)
SMD_w    <- as.numeric(escalc("SMD", m1i = warm_m, m2i = ctrl_m,
                              sd1i = warm_sd, sd2i = ctrl_sd,
                              n1i = n_w, n2i = n_w)$yi)

# Second case: same mean difference, but the SD grows in proportion to the mean
warm_sd_cv <- ctrl_sd * warm_m / ctrl_m
lnVR_cv  <- log(warm_sd_cv / ctrl_sd)
lnRoM_cv <- log(warm_m / ctrl_m)
lnCVR_cv <- as.numeric(escalc("CVR", m1i = warm_m, m2i = ctrl_m,
                              sd1i = warm_sd_cv, sd2i = ctrl_sd,
                              n1i = n_w, n2i = n_w, correct = FALSE)$yi)
```

:::callout-note
#### Key points
- lnVR compares the standard deviations of two groups. It describes change in variability on its own.
- lnCVR compares coefficients of variation. It is defined by lnVR and lnRoM, so it mixes changes in the mean with changes in variability.
- Analyze lnVR alongside lnRoM (or SMD). See [lnCVR](#sec-lnCVR) for when to add lnCVR as a sensitivity analysis.
:::

The most commonly used effect sizes concern *mean* relationships between variables.

However, *variability* is itself a meaningful dimension of reality, not merely noise [@Nakagawa2026-wm]. In ecological contexts, heterogeneity is considered a key driver of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning [@Stein2014-gj; @Levine2016-hb]. Likewise, in evolution, variability tells us important information about selective pressures which can either increase variation [@Buckley2016-sn; @O-Dea2016-jy] or reduce it [@Crispo2007-nf].

There are two main effect sizes for calculating variability between two groups (i.e., discrete predictors): **lnVR** and **lnCVR** [@Nakagawa2015-tq].

Throughout this page we use the Arctic willow warming example from [2.1](2.1-SMD-assumptions.qmd): *Salix arctica* aboveground biomass in an ambient control (10 g, SD 2 g) and a warming treatment (12 g, SD 3 g), with 20 plants per group. For this example, lnVR = `r round(lnVR_w, 3)`, lnRoM = `r round(lnRoM_w, 3)`, and Hedges' g = `r round(SMD_w, 2)`.

## lnVR {#sec-lnVR}

lnVR is the log-transformed ratio of the standard deviations of two groups:

$$
\mathrm{lnVR}=\ln\left(\frac{sd_1}{sd_2}\right),
$${#eq-lnvr}

where $sd_1$ is the treatment-group standard deviation and $sd_2$ is the control-group standard deviation. If group 1 is your treatment or experimental group:

- $\mathrm{lnVR}>0$: the treatment group is more variable than the control group;

- $\mathrm{lnVR}=0$: the groups have equal standard deviations;

- $\mathrm{lnVR}<0$: the treatment group is less variable.

For the willow example, $\mathrm{lnVR} = \ln(3/2) = `r round(lnVR_w, 3)`$.

#### Interpretation
lnVR can be back transformed to plain English by exponentiating (i.e., $e^{lnVR}$).

If we have an lnVR of 0.4: $e^{0.4}\approx1.5$. This indicates that the standard deviation of the treatment group is approximately 50% higher than the control group.

Combining an lnRoM or SMD meta-analysis of mean differences with an lnVR meta-analysis can provide a fuller description of biological change.

#### How to calculate
To calculate lnVR, use `measure="VR"` in `escalc` or `eff_size` in `metatools`. The tabs below show both:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## metafor

```{r}
escalc(measure = "VR",
       sd1i = 3, n1i = 20,
       sd2i = 2, n2i = 20,
       vtype = "LS2")
```

## metatools

```{r}
#| label: lnvr-metatools
eff_size(sd1 = 3, n1 = 20,
         sd2 = 2, n2 = 20,
         effect_type = "lnVR",
         verbose = FALSE)
```

:::

metatools uses the second-order variance by default, which metafor gives with `vtype = "LS2"`. The table compares the two packages.

```{r}
#| label: lnvr-comparison
#| echo: false
vr_mf <- escalc(measure = "VR", sd1i = 3, n1i = 20,
                sd2i = 2, n2i = 20, vtype = "LS2")
vr_mt <- eff_size(sd1 = 3, n1 = 20, sd2 = 2, n2 = 20,
                  effect_type = "lnVR", verbose = FALSE)
data.frame(package = c("metafor", "metatools"),
           yi = c(vr_mf$yi, vr_mt$yi),
           vi = c(vr_mf$vi, vr_mt$vi)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

Note that `escalc` applies a small-sample bias correction to lnVR by default. If you want the simple formula shown above, set `correct = FALSE`.

There is a paired version of lnVR as well, which requires an estimate of the correlation between group 1 and 2, which we can specify as 0.5 or 0.8 if it's unreported (which is typical, see [here](2.1-SMD-assumptions.qmd#sec-paired-designs)). Use this formula if groups 1 and 2 are paired, e.g., from paired plots, before-after experiments, and so on.

In `escalc` this is specified with the "VRC" measure:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| out-width: "70%"
escalc(measure = "VRC",
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.5,
       ni = 15, ri = 0.5)
```

:::callout-note
@Senior2026-oh recently demonstrated that using bivariate models with lnRoM and lnVR as response variables can increase statistical power to detect effects of treatments on both variation and mean responses. This is an interesting and little implemented method to incorporate both mean differences and variability into a single meta-analytic model.
:::


## lnCVR {#sec-lnCVR}

**lnCVR** is the *log-transformed coefficient of variation ratio*. Its definition formula (prior to small sample bias correction) is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lnCVR=\ln\left(\frac{sd_1/m_1}{sd_2/m_2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-lncvr}

This effect size **is** standardized by the mean. As such, this effect size cannot accept negative mean values, requiring positive, ratio-scale data like the [lnRoM effect size](2.1-SMD-assumptions.qmd). (Note that standard deviations can never be negative so **lnVR** is always calculable as long as standard deviations were reported, even if means are <0).

Importantly, lnCVR describes both mean differences between groups and differences in variability and has an exact mathematical relationship with **lnVR** and **lnRoM**:

$$
lnCVR = lnVR - lnRoM
$${#eq-lncvr-lnvr-lnrom}

For the willow example, $\mathrm{lnVR} - \mathrm{lnRoM} = `r round(lnVR_w, 3)` - `r round(lnRoM_w, 3)` = `r round(lnVR_w - lnRoM_w, 3)`$, which is the lnCVR we get directly from the formula (`r round(lnCVR_w, 3)`). We can check this with `escalc` using the warming means and SDs (m = 12 and 10 g, sd = 3 and 2 g, n = 20 per group):

```{r}
escalc(measure = "CVR",
       m1i = 12, m2i = 10,
       sd1i = 3, sd2i = 2,
       n1i = 20, n2i = 20, correct = FALSE)
```

Both packages return the bias-corrected lnCVR by default, and metafor gives the same second-order variance as metatools with `vtype = "LS2"`.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## metafor

```{r}
escalc(measure = "CVR",
       m1i = 12, m2i = 10,
       sd1i = 3, sd2i = 2,
       n1i = 20, n2i = 20,
       vtype = "LS2")
```

## metatools

```{r}
#| label: lncvr-metatools
eff_size(x1 = 12, sd1 = 3, n1 = 20,
         x2 = 10, sd2 = 2, n2 = 20,
         effect_type = "lnCVR",
         verbose = FALSE)
```

:::

The table compares the two packages.

```{r}
#| label: lncvr-comparison
#| echo: false
cvr_mf <- escalc(measure = "CVR", m1i = 12, m2i = 10,
                 sd1i = 3, sd2i = 2, n1i = 20, n2i = 20,
                 vtype = "LS2")
cvr_mt <- eff_size(x1 = 12, sd1 = 3, n1 = 20,
                   x2 = 10, sd2 = 2, n2 = 20,
                   effect_type = "lnCVR", verbose = FALSE)
data.frame(package = c("metafor", "metatools"),
           yi = c(cvr_mf$yi, cvr_mt$yi),
           vi = c(cvr_mf$vi, cvr_mt$vi)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

:::callout-important
Because **lnCVR** is defined by both **lnVR** and **lnRoM**, analyze lnVR alongside lnRoM (or SMD). Together, they describe both differences in variability and differences in mean relationships. For when to add lnCVR, see the discussion below.
:::

**lnCVR** is intended to account for a common biological pattern: groups with larger means often also have larger variances. However, dividing by the mean makes an implicit scaling assumption. In simple terms, it works most naturally when the standard deviation increases roughly in proportion to the mean. Equivalently, variance then increases roughly with the square of the mean.

That relationship differs among data types:

- **Approximately normal data with constant variance:** the standard deviation may stay similar as the mean changes. The coefficient of variation will then change mechanically with the mean.

- **Poisson count data:** variance equals the mean, so standard deviation increases with the square root of the mean rather than directly with the mean. The coefficient of variation therefore decreases as the mean increases.

- **Negative-binomial count data:** variance can increase much faster than the mean. At large means, the standard deviation may be close to proportional to the mean, but the relationship depends on the dispersion parameter.

- **Proportions and other bounded responses:** variance is constrained by the mean and commonly shrinks near the boundaries. The mean–variance relationship can therefore be strong and nonlinear.

For these reasons, do not choose lnCVR automatically. First plot or model the relationship between group means and standard deviations across the dataset. In all cases, analyze lnVR alongside lnRoM (or SMD). lnCVR is a sensitivity analysis: add it when *relative variability* is the question, and only if its assumed mean–variance scaling is plausible. If the results are different, these comparisons can help you understand **why**.

@fig-lnvr-lncvr-densities shows two cases. In panel A (our willow example), the warmed plants' SD grew more than their mean did: the SD went up `r round((warm_sd / ctrl_sd - 1) * 100)`% (2 g to 3 g), but the mean only went up `r round((warm_m / ctrl_m - 1) * 100)`% (10 g to 12 g). So both lnVR and lnCVR are above zero. In panel B, the SD grows by exactly the same proportion as the mean (2 g to `r warm_sd_cv` g, also `r round((warm_m / ctrl_m - 1) * 100)`%). So lnCVR is zero, while lnVR equals lnRoM.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lnvr-lncvr-densities
#| fig-cap: "Normal densities (curves, not raw data) for two pairs of groups. Panel A is the Arctic willow warming example: control 10 g (SD 2 g) and warmed 12 g (SD 3 g), with 20 plants per group. Panel B keeps the same means but sets the warmed SD to 2.4 g, so the coefficient of variation is unchanged. Blue solid curves are the control group and orange dashed curves are the warmed (treatment) group."
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side panels of density curves. Panel A shows a narrow blue control curve centered at 10 and a wider orange dashed warmed curve centered at 12. Panel B shows the same centers with a warmed curve only slightly wider than the control curve. Both panels share the same horizontal axis of biomass in grams."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: "100%"
cols <- c("Control" = "#0072B2", "Warmed (treatment)" = "#D55E00")
xs <- seq(2, 20, length.out = 400)

dens_df <- function(m_c, sd_c, m_t, sd_t, panel) {
  rbind(
    data.frame(x = xs, y = dnorm(xs, m_c, sd_c), group = "Control", panel = panel),
    data.frame(x = xs, y = dnorm(xs, m_t, sd_t), group = "Warmed (treatment)", panel = panel)
  )
}
dd <- rbind(
  dens_df(ctrl_m, ctrl_sd, warm_m, warm_sd, "A: Arctic willow (SD 3 g)"),
  dens_df(ctrl_m, ctrl_sd, warm_m, warm_sd_cv, "B: constant CV (SD 2.4 g)")
)

ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Control" = "solid", "Warmed (treatment)" = "dashed")) +
  labs(x = "Biomass (g)", y = "Density", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

#### How to calculate
This can be calculated in `escalc` with `measure = "CVR"`. This effect size requires the same statistical ingredients as SMD and lnRoM:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| out-width: "70%"
escalc(measure = "CVR",
       m1i = 12, m2i = 10,
       sd1i = 3, sd2i = 2,
       n1i = 20, n2i = 20)
```

There is a paired version of lnCVR as well. In `escalc` this is specified with `measure="CVRC"`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| out-width: "70%"
escalc(measure = "CVRC",
        m1i = 12, m2i = 10,
       sd1i = 3, sd2i = 2,
       ni = 20, ri = 0.5)
```
